## Fundamental Group of \(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S\)

**Answer.** \(\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S) \cong \mathbb{Z}\).

---

### Proof

Let \(S = \{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb{R}^3 : x^2+y^2=1\}\) be the unit circle in the \(xy\)-plane, viewed as lying in \(S^3 = \mathbb{R}^3\cup\{\infty\}\) (with \(\infty\notin S\)).

#### Step 1. Reduction to \(S^3\setminus S\)

Since \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^3\), we have \(S^3\setminus S = (\mathbb{R}^3\setminus S)\cup\{\infty\}\), i.e. \(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus S = (S^3\setminus S)\setminus\{\infty\}\). The space \(S^3\setminus S\) is an open 3-manifold, and \(\infty\) has a 3-ball neighborhood in \(S^3\setminus S\) disjoint from \(S\). Removing a single point from a 3-manifold does **not** change the fundamental group: every loop (image of \(S^1\), dimension 1) and every homotopy between loops (image of \(D^2\), dimension 2) can be perturbed by general position to avoid the point \(\infty\) (codimension \(3>2\)). Hence the inclusion
\[
\mathbb{R}^3\setminus S \;\hookrightarrow\; S^3\setminus S
\]
induces an isomorphism on \(\pi_1\). It suffices to compute \(\pi_1(S^3\setminus S)\).

#### Step 2. A tubular neighborhood and its complement

Let \(N\) be a closed tubular neighborhood of \(S\) in \(S^3\), chosen thin enough (fiber radius \(<1\)) so that \(N\) is a solid torus \(S^1\times D^2\) with core \(S\), and so that \(N\) is disjoint from the \(z\)-axis and from \(\infty\).

The unknot \(S\) bounds the disk \(D=\{(x,y,0):x^2+y^2\le 1\}\). A standard fact (the genus-1 Heegaard splitting of \(S^3\)) is that the complement of a tubular neighborhood of an unknot is again a solid torus. Concretely, set
\[
C \;=\; \{(0,0,z):z\in\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{\infty\}\;\subset\;S^3,
\]
the \(z\)-axis together with the point at infinity; this is a circle in \(S^3\) (a line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) closed up by \(\infty\)) that links \(S\) once (it pierces the disk \(D\) transversely in exactly one point). Since \(C\cap N=\varnothing\), we have \(C\subset S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)\). A tubular neighborhood of \(C\) is exactly \(S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)\); thus
\[
M \;:=\; S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)
\]
is a solid torus with core \(C\).

#### Step 3. Deformation retraction

The space \(S^3\setminus S\) deformation retracts onto \(S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)=M\): inside the deleted tubular neighborhood \(N\setminus S\), each punctured normal disk \(D^2\setminus\{0\}\) deformation retracts onto its boundary \(\partial D^2\subset\partial N\), and this fiberwise retraction extends by the identity on \(M\). Hence
\[
S^3\setminus S \;\simeq\; M.
\]

The solid torus \(M\) in turn deformation retracts onto its core circle \(C\cong S^1\). Therefore
\[
S^3\setminus S \;\simeq\; S^1,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\pi_1(S^3\setminus S)\cong\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb{Z}.
\]

#### Step 4. The generator

Under the retractions above, the generator of \(\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus S)\cong\mathbb{Z}\) is represented by a **meridian** of \(S\): a small circle in a normal disk to \(S\) that winds once around \(S\) (linking number \(1\) with \(S\)). On the common boundary torus \(\partial N=\partial M\), this meridian of \(N\) becomes the longitude (core direction) of the complementary solid torus \(M\), hence it represents the generator of \(\pi_1(M)\cong\mathbb{Z}\). A loop with linking number \(k\) with \(S\) represents \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\).

#### Conclusion

Combining Steps 1 and 3,
\[
\boxed{\pi_1\!\left(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus S\right)\;\cong\;\mathbb{Z}},
\]
freely generated by a meridian of the circle \(S\) (equivalently, by any loop of linking number \(1\) with \(S\)).

M \;:=\; S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(N)
